s: The Bill of Rights originally bound only the federal government (Barron v. Baltimore, 1833).
After the Fourteenth Amendment, the Slaughter-House Cases (1873) read the Privileges or Immunities Clause narrowly, so incorporation developed through the Due Process Clause instead.
Beginning with Gitlow v. New York (1925, speech) and accelerating in the Warren Court, the Court selectively incorporated nearly every Bill of Rights guarantee.
It asked whether each right is "fundamental to our scheme of ordered liberty" or "deeply rooted in this Nation's history and tradition" (Duncan v. Louisiana, 1968; McDonald v. City of Chicago, 2010).
